tracks.title: The machinery of the schedule
tracks.text: Lesson 05 point 5 — orchestration. A deep dive… under agents. The parent lesson sold you one phrase — a model… on a schedule. [curious] And that word, schedule, hides an engine. The machinery of the schedule. A schedule worth trusting has to survive crashes… redeploys… idle stretches… and the moment you run a second agent beside the first. That engine is what this page is. About four hundred lines of tick loop… plus a state machine you declare in org. And here's the surprise that runs through everything — almost none of it… is AI. It's a careful loop, a few files on disk, and a state machine in plain text.

tracks.title: Cron is not a colleague
tracks.text: First — cron is not a colleague. The naive version is one line. A cron job… that calls a model. It works in the demo… and fails in production, in five specific ways. First — the schedule dies with the run. The model call throws, the process that scheduled it goes down, and your standing agent is now a stopped agent. Second — a redeploy resets the clock. You push a fix at two… the agent due at two oh five now fires a fresh hour later. Every deploy skips a beat. Third — you pay for idle polls. Nothing to do this tick… but the model still gets called to discover that. A full bill… to be told nothing. Fourth — the days have no shape. The agent does stuff every tick, with no sense that mornings add work and afternoons audit it. And fifth — two of them grab the same task. The instant you run a second agent on the same board, both reach for the top ticket… and you paid twice for one result. [curious] Orchestration is the answer to all five. And almost none of the answer… is intelligence.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. Orchestration is the deterministic skeleton… around non-deterministic work. Three parts. First — a tick engine that owns when an agent runs. Second — a lifecycle, declared in org, that owns what kind of work each tick does. Third — a claims protocol, that says who took which task. One worker… is one agent… is one cadence. And the whole design is a single split, written right into the code as a comment — org owns the spec… this module just interprets and steps it. The runtime is rigid on purpose. It decides timing, position, gates, and retries… and it never improvises. The intelligence lives inside a state, where the agent decides what the work actually is. [excited] Determinism on the outside… judgment on the inside.

tracks.title: Anatomy of a tick
tracks.text: Anatomy of a tick. Picture one heartbeat as a flow. A worker — one per agent — gets a tick message, and runs a fixed sequence. First it records the time, so a restart can do the arithmetic later. Then, if git-ops is on, it pulls the tenant's origin… so a push from anywhere becomes live within one tick. Then it consults the lifecycle — which state am I in? If that state is gated by a minimum interval that hasn't elapsed… it's a no-op, hold position, and schedule the next beat. Otherwise — the green box at the center — it runs the agent definition, inside a killable task, under a fifteen-minute wall clock. And whatever comes back maps to one of four outcomes — done… no-work… failed… or killed — each routing to its own next delay, and then… send-after, the next tick is scheduled. Two safety properties are doing quiet work in that picture. The run lives in a linked task the worker can shut down with a brutal kill — so a hang is bounded at fifteen minutes, and a crash never takes the worker down with it. [excited] The schedule outlives the run. That's failure mode number one… solved. And the run is the very same call path as a public request — the standing agent and a one-off run execute identically.

tracks.title: A day declared in org
tracks.text: A day declared in org. A schedule that just fires every hour has no shape. The lifecycle gives the day a shape — a deterministic state machine, declared in org, executed one transition per tick. Let me read you the spec. It opens with a start line — hash-plus-start, wake-add. Then four states, each a heading. First… wake-add — kind, wake — repeat, three — next, wake-audit. Second… wake-audit — kind wake — next, rem. Third… rem — kind, rem — next, wake-plan — and a minimum interval of ten minutes. And fourth… wake-plan — kind wake — next, back to wake-add. Now read it as a loop. The start line names the entry state. Kind wake runs the model. Kind rem is a quiet beat — it hands off to the dream phase, and never calls the model. Repeat three means do wake-add three successful ticks before taking its edge. And minimum interval, ten minutes, on rem… is a time gate — that state refuses to run until ten minutes have passed since it last did. So picture the state diagram as a ring. Wake-add loops on itself while hits are under three… then on the third success, an arrow to wake-audit… audit to rem… rem, through its ten-minute gate, to wake-plan… and wake-plan closes the ring back to wake-add. Add three times… audit once… rest… plan… and around again. The skeleton is deterministic. But what the agent does inside wake-add stays non-deterministic — that's the definition's job, not the engine's. And the spec file is re-read every tick, kept deliberately dumb… so a spec you hot-edit is picked up next beat. [curious] You can change the shape of a live agent's day… without restarting it.

tracks.title: Four outcomes, one rule each
tracks.text: Four outcomes… one rule each. Every tick ends in exactly one of four, and each does a single predictable thing to the agent's position — the pair, state and hits. Here is the verdict of each. First — done. Real work happened. Hits plus one… and at the repeat count, take the next edge and reset hits. Hot cadence. Second — no-work. The result began with the literal words no-work. Collapse the remaining repeats, take the next edge now, and back off. Third — failed. The run errored. Hold — retry the same state next tick. And fourth — killed. The run blew the fifteen-minute wall clock. Same as failed — hold, retry the same state. The headline is those last two. A crash, or a timeout… holds position. [excited] The cadence clock is never lost. Your place in the day is durable against the worst thing a run can do. And the no-work rule has a subtlety worth stating exactly. It is a fast-forward of repeats… never a skip of states. If there's genuinely nothing to add, wake-add collapses its remaining repeats and moves on — but every state in the declared order still runs. The audit still happens. The rest still happens. The engine speeds through empty repeats… without ever letting a state get skipped.

tracks.title: Cadence that survives the machine
tracks.text: Now — cadence that survives the machine. A depth rung, skippable… but it's where a model on a schedule becomes trustworthy. The agent's whole sense of time lives in three tiny files on disk. Let me name them. First… keeper-last-run — it holds the unix time of the last tick, and it preserves the catch-up math across a restart. Second… lifecycle-pos — it literally contains the words wake-add, two — and it preserves your place, the second of three adds. Third… lifecycle-ran, per state — the last time a gated state ran, which preserves the minimum-interval clock. The catch-up arithmetic is one expression — the next delay is the max of sixty seconds… and the interval minus elapsed time. If an hourly agent was forty minutes into its hour when you redeployed… it waits the remaining twenty. Not a fresh hour. The sixty-second floor is a boot grace, so a restart loop can't hammer the model. [excited] Failure mode number two — the reset clock — solved by reading a file. Two more details earn their keep. The current state is mirrored into process memory, so the public plane can read where an agent is in its day… without a blocking call — and that matters, because a tick runs synchronously, so asking a busy worker directly would make you wait the whole run. And a never-run gated state reads as infinitely elapsed… so its gate starts open.

tracks.title: The price of idleness
tracks.text: The price of idleness. Another depth rung — and the one that costs real money. Failure mode number three… paying for idle polls… gets its own mechanism. The convention is blunt. An agent with nothing to do ends its run with output that begins with the literal word… no-work. The engine reads that, and instead of running the next tick at full cadence… it backs off, exponentially. Here is the schedule, for a continuous worker on the default forty-five-second breather. At streak zero — forty-five seconds. Streak one — one minute. Streak two — two minutes. Streak three — four minutes. Streak four — eight minutes. Streak five — sixteen minutes. And streak six and beyond — thirty minutes, the cap. The verdict of that row — an idle agent quiets itself from roughly eighty model calls an hour… down to two. And the recovery is instant. A single done resets the streak, and snaps the agent straight back to hot cadence. [excited] It sleeps deeper the longer it's idle… and wakes fully the moment there's work. So — doesn't a standing agent cost a fortune doing nothing? No. Because doing nothing… is the one thing it gets cheap at.

tracks.title: Many workers, one box
tracks.text: Many workers… one box. Failure mode number five appears the instant you run two agents. The engine runs a set of them from one manifest. Let me read a two-member one. First member — wren. Its definition, a writer. A lifecycle. And an interval of ten minutes. Second member — moss. Its definition, an editor. No lifecycle — so plain interval ticks. And an interval of twenty minutes. Each member gets a full, independent worker — its own definition, its own lifecycle, its persistence namespaced by name. They tick in parallel, with no shared cadence state. Two things keep that from becoming chaos. First, a stagger — the i-th worker's first tick is delayed by thirty seconds times its index, so they don't all hit the model at boot. Second… a concurrency gate. A counting semaphore, default max two, that every run must pass through. Picture it as a conversation. Wren asks the gate to acquire — a slot is free, granted — and wren runs, holding a slot. Moss asks to acquire — slots full — so moss parks in a first-in-first-out queue. Now wren's run blows its fifteen-minute wall clock… and here's the key beat — wren still releases its slot, in an after-clause, even on timeout. The gate hands that slot straight to the queue head… and moss begins. [excited] A wedged worker can never deadlock the others. The fuller manifest grammar belongs to the fleets deep dive — here, just the shape.

tracks.title: Claims, not locks
tracks.text: Now the subtle one — claims, not locks. Two agents share a board. What stops them grabbing the same task? The deliberate answer — the runtime locks… nothing. Claiming is a definition-level protocol, not a runtime mutex. Picture the sequence. Wren reads the board — task seven is up next. Wren commits to git — task seven, now doing, agent wren — and only then does the work. Moss ticks. The first thing moss does is pull. And git tells moss — task seven is already doing, claimed by wren. So moss takes task eight instead. The runtime's job is narrower, and stronger, than locking. It isolates runs — each worker its own workdir and state — and it throttles them through the gate. Coordination correctness lives in the definition… and the board… exactly where the non-deterministic interior of a state already lives. The git commit makes the claim visible, auditable, and revertible — a social protocol, the way a person grabs a ticket off the wall before starting. [curious] It narrows the race. It does not, by itself, eliminate it.

tracks.title: Where the edges are
tracks.text: Where the edges are — the honesty section. This engine is small and rigid… and its limits come from exactly that. First — claims are unenforced. A badly written definition that works before it pulls can double-grab a task. The protocol makes a collision visible — it doesn't make it impossible. Second — failed states retry forever. A state that keeps erroring holds position and retries every beat. There's no poison-state escape beyond the backoff slowing it down. Third — the gate caps the box, not fairness. It bounds how many runs hit the model at once, and serves its queue first-in-first-out — no per-agent fairness beyond that order. Fourth — minimum interval is elapsed time, not a calendar. A gated state fires when enough wall-clock has passed… it is not every weekday at nine. For calendar scheduling, you want the workflow layer's timestamps. And fifth — one box. The workers run on a single engine. There is no cross-machine coordination — scaling past one box… is not this design.

tracks.title: Back up to agents
tracks.text: So that's orchestration. The deterministic skeleton around non-deterministic work. A tick engine that owns when… a lifecycle in org that owns what kind… and a claims protocol committed to git, that says who. A crash holds your place. A redeploy resumes mid-cadence. An idle agent quiets itself. And nobody locks anything. [curious] This whole page was the when… around the agent's what. The way back up is short. The parent is lesson five — agents — the model this schedules, the worker with tenure. Read it, and everything here is just the clock around it.
